sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Monetization**: The Mughal economy saw high levels of monetization, with the **Silver Rupee** (introduced by Sher Shah Suri, standardized by Akbar) serving as the universal medium of exchange.
• **Market Integration**: Trade was facilitated by a hierarchy of markets: **Qasbas** (small towns), **Mandis** (wholesale markets), and **Peths/Hats** (periodic rural markets).
• **Merchant Classes**: Trade was dominated by specialized communities like **Banias**, **Khatris**, and **Multanis**, who operated through sophisticated credit instruments.
• **Key Metric**: The **Hundi** (bill of exchange) was the backbone of inland trade, allowing for the transfer of large sums of money without physical movement of bullion.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Road Connectivity**: Development of the Shahi Sadak (Grand Trunk Road) connecting Sonargaon to Attock.
• **Standardization**: Uniformity in weights and measures enforced by the Kotwal in urban centers.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Excessive transit duties (Rahdari), lack of uniform currency in remote areas, and insecurity of routes.
• **Solutions**: Imperial firmans (decrees) issued by Aurangzeb to abolish illegal cesses (Abwabs).

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'H-S-B' (Hundi, Sarraf, Banjara).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Hundi (Credit), Sarraf (Banking), Banjara (Logistics/Transport).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses 'Rahdari' (illegal transit duty) with 'Zakat' (religious tax). Remember: Rahdari was a secular transit tax often declared illegal by emperors.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Proto-industrialization' when discussing the Mughal textile trade and its integration with inland markets.

keyTakeaways: The Mughal economy was highly monetized with a sophisticated credit system (Hundis).
Trade was heavily dependent on the Banjara caravans for bulk movement of grain.
State intervention was dual-natured: providing infrastructure (Sarais) while simultaneously hindering trade through arbitrary transit duties (Rahdari).
